stem: A 22-year-old man eats sausage from an expired and bloated can. A day later he develops trouble swallowing, muscle weakness, blurred vision, constipation, and dry mouth. On examination he is found to have decreased deep tendon reflexes. Which of the following is the toxin’s correct mechanism of action?

options.text: Inhibition of degradation of acetylcholine at cholinergic receptors
options.html: Inhibition of degradation of acetylcholine at cholinergic receptors

options.text: Inhibition of intracellular fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles
options.html: Inhibition of intracellular fusion of acetylcholine-containing vesicles

options.text: Inhibition of the binding of acetylcholine to its receptor
options.html: Inhibition of the binding of acetylcholine to its receptor

explanation: Botulinum toxin may be distributed from the gastrointestinal tract or lungs to cholinergic nerve endings where it blocks the release of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. It does this by inhibiting the intracellular fusion of acetylcholinecontaining vesicles to the nerve-terminal membrane for release into the synaptic cleft. This leads to flaccid paralysis that progresses until the respiratory muscles cease to contract. After ingestion, symptoms of blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, dry mouth, constipation, muscle weakness, and shortness of breath, may occur within 18-36 hours. Normal release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction is mediated a complex called SNARE which includes synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, and syntaxin. These allow the acetylcholine containing vesicle to fuse to cell membrane prior to release. Botulinum toxin enters the cell and cleaves SNARE proteins, which prevents fusion of the acetylcholine vesicle, and hence its release.
rationales:
Sarin is a neurotoxin that potently inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing continual transmission of nerve impulses and inability to control respiratory muscles. This is not the mechanism for botulinum toxin.
Answer C: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants such as rocuronium are competitive acetylcholine receptor inhibitors, effectively preventing the contraction of respiratory muscles. This is not the mechanism for botulinum toxin.
bottomLine: Botulinum toxin can cause symptoms of muscle paralysis by preventing the release of acetylcholine-containing vesicles from the axon terminal into the synaptic cleft.
trueLearnInsight: Botulinum toxin acts inside the axon terminal at the neuromuscular junction. Tetanus toxin travels via retrograde axonal transport to the central nervous system where it acts.

stem: Which of the following left-ventricular mechanical events corresponds with the electrical R wave on ECG?
explanation: The closing of the mitral valve corresponds with the electrical R wave of the QRS complex. The cardiac cycle is depicted in Figure 1 below with respect to the left heart. This tracing may be derived during a left heart catheterization. It is divided into electrical events according to the electrocardiogram and corresponding mechanical events. These events include the opening and closing of the mitral and aortic valves in conjunction with pressure changes within the left atrium, left ventricle, and the aorta. A similar tracing may be illustrated with lower pressures from the right-heart involving the right atrium, right ventricle, and the main pulmonary artery. Figure 1. The cardiac cycle as depicted from the left side of the heart. The R wave signifies the beginning of left-ventricular systole, where the mitral valve closes and left ventricle (LV) isovolumetric contraction begins. The pressure in the LV builds until it exceeds the aortic pressure. The aortic valve then opens (immediately after QRS), isovolumetric contraction ends, and the LV ejects stroke volume into the aorta. Once the LV pressure falls below the aortic pressure, the aortic valve closes (end of T wave repolarization) and LV isovolumetric relaxation begins. The LV pressure continues to fall until it equals the left atrial pressure, and the mitral valve opens. MV = mitral valve, LVP = left ventricle pressure, LAP = left atrial pressure, a = left atrial contraction, c = closed MV bulges into left atrium at start of LV systole, v = left atrial filling, AoP = aortic pressure, AoV = aortic valve, P-QRST = ECG wave complex, IC = isovolumetric contraction, IR = isovolumetric relaxation. Answers A & C: Once the LVP falls below the AoP, the AoV closes, LV isovolumetric relaxation begins, and ventricular diastole ensues. This corresponds with the end of T wave repolarization on ECG. The LVP continues to fall until it equals the LAP, the MV opens, and isovolumetric relaxation ends. The LV begins to fill and the cycle continues.
rationales: The R wave signifies the beginning of LV systole, where the MV closes and LV isovolumetric contraction begins, and LVP begins to exceed LAP. The pressure in the LV builds until it exceeds AoP, the AoV then opens, isovolumetric contraction ends, and the LV ejects stroke volume into the aorta. This occurs directly after the QRS complex on ECG.
bottomLine: The closing of the mitral valve corresponds with the electrical R wave of the QRS complex.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cardiac Cycle: ECG" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 724. Kaplan, Essentials of Cardiac Anesthesia, 1st edition, pp. 23-25.

stem: Which of the following BEST describes the mechanism of action of cytochrome p450?
explanation: Cytochrome p450 is a heme protein that utilizes molecular oxygen to oxidize organic compounds. Cytochrome p450 is not a single enzyme, but rather consists of a group of closely related proteins that are embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum. The structure of cytochrome p450 consists of iron (Fe), which serves as a binding site for oxygen molecules. Metabolism by cytochrome p450 has been extensively studied, and is involved in the oxidation of thousands of diverse drugs and chemicals. One atom of molecular oxygen is used to oxidize the drug, while the other atom is combined with hydrogen atoms from NADPH to form water. The liver is the principal site for drug metabolism. For many drugs, metabolism occurs in two phases. Phase I involves modifying the drug through oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis. These reactions typically inactivate the drug. Phase II involves conjugation, where a molecule (glucuronic acid, sulfate) is added to the drug to make it more easily excreted from the kidneys and liver. Cytochrome p450 is the most important enzyme system in phase I and catalyzes the oxidation of many drugs.
rationales:
Conjugation is part of phase II metabolism, where molecules are added to the drug to make it more readily excreted. Cytochrome p450 is involved with phase I oxidation.
Answer B: Hydrolysis is part of phase I, but is not mediated by p450 group.
Answer D: Reduction is part of phase I metabolism. However, cytochrome p450 catalyzes oxidation in phase I.
bottomLine: Cytochrome p450 is involved in phase I metabolism by oxidizing many drugs.
trueLearnInsight: Chronic barbiturate use increases cytochrome p450 activity. As a result, the metabolism of drugs by p450 is increased (as seen with benzodiazepines).

stem: Which of the following variables will result in an INCREASED functional residual capacity?
explanation: Functional residual capacity (FRC) goes up with increased height and advanced age. FRC will go down with increased weight, decreased height, and in females compared with males. A decrease in FRC can also be seen in lung disease such as idiopathic fibrosis, pneumoconiosis, and different forms of granulomatosis and vasculitis. Following a lung resection a reduction in FRC will be seen; occasionally the remaining lung will expand to fill in some of the space left. FRC increases with age because of loss of elastic lung tissue, which lessens the contractile force of the lung and moves the balancing point between the outward force of the chest wall and the inward force of the lung to higher lung volume. In patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), FRC increases faster over the years than in normal subjects because of an effect of chronic air trapping and more severe loss of elastic tissue (in particular in emphysema). Functional residual capacity is the amount of air that is left in the lungs after a normal expiration. It is approximately 30 mL/kg in an average adult. FRC is dependent on age, sex, height and weight. The volume is determined by the balance of the inward forces of the lungs against the outward force of the chest wall. The inward forces are referred to as the “elastic recoil” and consist of the lung tissue and the contractile forces of the airway smooth muscle and surface tension of the alveoli. The outward force is exerted by the ribs, joints and muscles. If the alveoli completely collapsed after exhalation, the amount of force that would be required to reopen them would be tremendous thus a residual amount of air must remain. For newborns, the PaO2 in the first few days after birth rapidly increases. The PaO2 initially is low due to a decrease in FRC and fluid-filled alveoli. The FRC in neonates increases over the first few days of life until day 4, at which point it reaches adult levels. Answers B & C: FRC will go down with increased weight, decreased height, and in females compared with males.
bottomLine: Functional residual capacity increases with age due to loss of elastic lung tissue which acts as an inward force pulling the lungs closed. An increase will also be seen with increased height secondary to the larger lungs compared to short counterparts.
trueLearnInsight: Other causes of low FRC are PANGOS: Pregnancy, Ascites, Neonatal, General anesthesia, Obesity, Supine position.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Increased FRC: Causes (B)" Miller’s Anesthesia. 7th Edition. Respiratory Physiology. Pages 363.

stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the termination of an action potential in a neuron?
explanation: Calcium ion movement does not play a role in neuronal action potential termination. Action potentials are brief, localized depolarizations on cell membranes used to transmit an electrical signal across a distance. Neurons generally have a resting membrane potential of -60 to -70 mV. A localized membrane depolarization that surpasses a certain threshold is able to then generate and propagate an action potential. This initial depolarization causes voltage-gated sodium channels to open from their closed state, allowing rapid influx of sodium ions which further depolarize the membrane to activate more local and downstream sodium channels in a positive feedback mechanism. At its peak, an action potential generates a cell membrane voltage of nearly +40 mV. Termination of the action potential occurs primarily via two mechanisms. First, the voltage-gated sodium channels terminate their positive feedback by self-inactivation within milliseconds of opening. Inactivated sodium channels do not allow further sodium ion influx despite a still depolarized membrane. Second, both voltage-gated and voltage-independent potassium channels open in response to depolarization and allow potassium efflux out the cell. Combined, these effects result in neuron membrane repolarization back towards the resting potential. During this time, the sodium channels transition from an inactivated state (unable to potentiate an action potential) to a closed state (ready to open upon threshold stimulation). However, the potassium channels are slower to close than the sodium channels and overshoot the repolarization, causing a brief period of hyperpolarization. The cell membrane returns to its resting potential due to numerous other ion channels/pumps, namely the sodium-potassium-ATPase.
rationales:
This is the combined effect of steps one and two for action potential termination.
Answer B: This is the first step in action potential termination.
Answer D: This is the second step in action potential termination.
bottomLine: A neuron action potential is terminated by membrane repolarization caused by the inactivation and then closing of voltage-dependent sodium channels and the opening of potassium channels that promote potassium efflux.
trueLearnInsight: Local anesthetics block nerve impulse transmission by reversibly binding to the intracellular portion of the voltage-gated sodium channels and thereby preventing sodium ion influx.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Nerve AP termination mechanism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 218-220, 532-534.

stem: Which of the following statements about aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis is TRUE?

options.text: Anaerobic glycolysis produces approximately 30 more ATP than aerobic glycolysis per molecule of glucose
options.html: Anaerobic glycolysis produces approximately 30 more ATP than aerobic glycolysis per molecule of glucose

options.text: Both processes utilize glucose as the starting substrate
options.html: Both processes utilize glucose as the starting substrate

options.text: The end products of anaerobic glycolysis are carbon dioxide and water
options.html: The end products of anaerobic glycolysis are carbon dioxide and water

options.text: The majority of ATP generated during aerobic glycolysis is produced in the cytoplasm
options.html: The majority of ATP generated during aerobic glycolysis is produced in the cytoplasm

explanation: Both aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis start with the same initial reactions that convert glucose to pyruvate. Most human cells utilize two primary mechanisms for the generation of ATP: anaerobic glycolysis (anaerobic metabolism) in the absence of adequate oxygen and aerobic glycolysis (aerobic metabolism) in the presence of adequate oxygen. Both types of metabolism begin the same: conversion of one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate within the cytoplasm. This process consumes two ATP but produces 4 ATP (net +2 ATP). At this point, the two processes diverge. In anaerobic metabolism, the two pyruvate molecules are converted into lactate in order to regenerate NAD+ consumed in the initial stages of glycolysis. This process occurs without any additional ATP formation and is thus not efficient at the cellular level. Aerobic metabolism utilizes three additional major processes in order to increase the ATP yield per molecule of glucose. First, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion where it undergoes conversion to acetyl CoA via the Link reaction. Second, the acetyl CoA then enters the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) where multiple key substrates are generated (GTP, FADH2, and NADH) and carbon dioxide is released as a waste product. Finally, the FADH2 and NADH molecules undergo oxidative phosphorylation within the mitochondrial inner membrane. Within this process, the FADH2 and NADH donate high-energy electrons that proceed down an electron transport chain, reduce oxygen gas to water, and ultimately generate approximately 30 ATP (per molecule of glucose). The figure below summarizes anaerobic and aerobic metabolism. Note that the number of ATP generated during oxidative phosphorylation during aerobic glycolysis (34 in the figure below) is actually variable and may be between 30-36.
rationales:
Anaerobic metabolism produces approximately 30 fewer ATP than aerobic metabolism per molecule of glucose.
Answer B: Anaerobic and aerobic metabolism both use glucose as the initial substrate.
Answer C: Carbon dioxide and water are the end products of aerobic metabolism. Lactate is the primary end product of anaerobic metabolism (hence lactate production when oxygen does not get to tissues).
Answer D: The majority of ATP generated during aerobic metabolism is produced in the mitochondrion (i.e. the powerhouse of the cell). Only two molecules of ATP are generated in the cytoplasm.
bottomLine: Aerobic metabolism produces approximately 16 times the ATP of anaerobic metabolism. The additional ATP is produced within the mitochondrion via the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Both anaerobic and aerobic metabolism start with glucose, but anaerobic metabolism generates lactate while aerobic metabolism produces carbon dioxide and water.
trueLearnInsight: In anaerobic glycolysis, the free energy of oxidation (NADH to NAD+) is wasted as heat, whereas in aerobic glycolysis 2.5-3 ATP are produced per NADH.

stem: Which of the following would decrease left ventricle coronary perfusion pressure?

options.text: Decrease in pulmonary artery occlusion pressure
options.html: Decrease in pulmonary artery occlusion pressure

options.text: Increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure
options.html: Increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure

explanation: An increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) results in greater compression of subendocardial blood vessels, impedes coronary blood flow (CBF), and lowers coronary perfusion pressure (CPP). Coronary perfusion pressure of the left ventricle is defined as aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) minus LVEDP: CPPLV = AoDP – LVEDP A myocardial pressure-volume loop (see below) may be utilized to illustrate key parameters of the cardiac cycle. Diastolic filling occurs as the left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV) increases towards the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV). The difference in these volumes ultimately translates into the ventricular stroke volume (SV). The corresponding pressure of the LVEDV is the LVEDP. The LV pressure increases from the LVEDP towards the AoDP during systole. The aortic valve opens once the LV pressure exceeds AoDP and the ejection period commences. Blood is ejected into the aorta until the LV pressure equilibrates with the aortic systolic pressure (AoSP). The aortic valve then closes and the mitral valve opens. Coronary perfusion then occurs during diastole and ventricular relaxation. Normal myocardial pressure-volume loop. LVESV = left ventricular end-systolic volume, LVEDV = left ventricular end-diastolic volume, LVESP = left ventricular end-systolic pressure, LVEDP = left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, CPP = coronary perfusion pressure, AoDP = aortic diastolic pressure, AoSP = aortic systolic pressure, SV = stroke volume.
rationales:
Lower values of LVEDP improve cardiac perfusion by reducing the resistance to blood flow through the coronary arteries and branches. A simultaneous reduction in myocardial oxygen demand occurs due to a reduction in ventricular volume and wall tension. Preload reduction decreases ventricular stretch (wall tension) which lowers LVEDP, and therefore increases CPP.
Answer B: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP) may be used as a proxy for LVEDP. A decrease in PAOP is generally regarded as a decrease in LVEDP, which leads to an increase in CPP.
Answer C: An increase in AoDP increases CPP.
bottomLine: CPPLV = AoDP - LVEDP. Hemodynamic variables that increase LVEDP will decrease CPP. Autoregulation of CBF is compromised with coronary stenosis. Autoregulation fails first in the subendocardium, resulting in subendocardial ischemia and ST segment depression.

stem: A 60-year-old male is scheduled to undergo laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The patient has a history of type I diabetes mellitus complicated by gastroparesis and peripheral neuropathy. Which of the following is TRUE?

options.text: Metoclopramide will decrease the gastric volume but has no effect on pH
options.html: Metoclopramide will decrease the gastric volume but has no effect on pH

options.text: Ranitidine will decrease the gastric volume and pH
options.html: Ranitidine will decrease the gastric volume and pH

options.text: Sodium citrate can be given to rapidly decrease the gastric pH
options.html: Sodium citrate can be given to rapidly decrease the gastric pH

options.text: Sucralfate will significantly increase the gastric pH
options.html: Sucralfate will significantly increase the gastric pH

explanation: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist with peripheral cholinergic agonism that can be used to decrease the gastric volume in patients with impaired gastric emptying. Metoclopramide decreases gastric volume by its prokinetic effect, increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, but has no effect on gastric pH. It is contraindicated in patients with pheochromocytoma. It should also be used with caution in patients with Parkinson disease due to the risk of causing rigidity and exacerbation of extrapyramidal symptoms. Metoclopramide is also used perioperatively as an antiemetic, though it has weak antiemetic action.
rationales:
Ranitidine will increase, not decrease the gastric pH. It has no effect on gastric volume.
Answer C: Sodium citrate is a weak base and reacts with hydrochloric acid in the stomach to increase, not decrease, the gastric pH.
Answer D: Sucralfate does not affect the gastric volume and only has a local effect on gastric pH.
bottomLine: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, enhances gastric emptying in patients who have slowed gastric emptying, and decreases gastric fluid volume. Unfortunately, its antiemetic properties are weak.
trueLearnInsight: Current guidelines recommend using a higher dose (25-50 mg) of metoclopramide when used as an antiemetic as this medication has weak antiemetic properties. Additionally, the "Society for Ambulatory Anesthesia Guidelines for the management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting do not recommend metoclopramide as an antiemetic for a patient who has received prophylactic ondansetron intraoperatively."

stem: Which of the following is NOT a metabolic effect of the stress response during the operative period?
explanation: Insulin levels are decreased during the stress response. The metabolic effects of the stress response act to mobilize glucose stores available and increased insulin would not contribute to this. Following any kind of trauma, the body reacts in an organized pattern through hormonal and metabolic changes. This is often termed the stress response and the effects are seen in every organ system. This response developed in order to survive, however in modern-day it can be detrimental, especially in the perioperative period. Numerous studies have been devoted to finding a way to diminish this response and it appears the degree of stress response activation is proportional to the degree of injury (i.e. larger surgeries result in higher degree of activation). When the body is under stress, the endocrine system ramps up secretion of a variety of hormones. The hypothalamic-pituitary axis and the sympathetic nervous system are activated by afferent nerve input from the area of trauma or injury. Activation of the sympathetic nervous system will cause an increased secretion of catecholamines from the adrenal medulla (norepinephrine is the primary neurotransmitter). Activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis will result in increased secretion of certain hormones from the pituitary which will act on the target organs. In review, the hormones released from the pituitary gland include adrenocorticotrophic hormone (corticotropin, ACTH), arginine vasopressin (AVP), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), as well as thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), growth hormone (GH), prolactin, and oxytocin. In response to stress, GH, ACTH, prolactin, and AVP all have an increased secretion while TSH, LH, and FSH are unchanged (although some studies report an increased secretion of TSH). The increased pituitary secretion will cause an increase in the target organ secretion: cortisol and aldosterone in the adrenal cortex, glucagon in the pancreas. Cortisol promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, lipolysis, and ketone body production. Protein catabolism is stimulated during stress predominantly from the skeletal muscle but also through some visceral muscle protein breakdown. Fat metabolism occurs mainly through lipolysis (conversion of triglycerides to glycerol and fatty acids). In addition, glucagon also promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In the perioperative period, insulin levels vary depending on multiple factors. In the operative period, the pancreas releases less insulin and a certain degree of peripheral insulin resistance is observed. Insulin is a key hormone that is usually secreted in response to hyperglycemia, promoting glucose utilization in the cells. During the stress of surgery, the islet cells of the pancreas, where insulin is made, are inhibited secondary to catecholamines. The metabolic results of this endocrine response include mobilization of energy stores along with alterations in salt and water metabolism. Blood glucose concentrations increase during stress and the degree of glucose elevation is related to the intensity of the surgery. Postoperatively, insulin concentrations escalate because of the increases in plasma glucose that occurred during the operative period and the epinephrine-induced beta-adrenergic stimulation. Several hormones alter salt and water metabolism in order to preserve adequate body fluid volumes. Arginine vasopressin promotes water retention and its secretion is increased for several days following surgery. Anesthesia likely has profound effects on the stress response associated with surgery. Opioids suppress the hypothalamic and pituitary hormone secretion. Regional anesthesia is thought to decrease the stress response but findings have been conflicting.
rationales:
Lipolysis is increased during the stress response due to increased catecholamine secretion. Triglycerides are metabolized to fatty acids and glycerol which is a gluconeogenic substrate.
Answer B: Insulin resistance occurs later in the stress response. It is thought that it occurs secondary to a defect in the insulin receptor-intracellular signaling pathway.
Answer C: Glycogenolysis, which is the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, is increased during the stress response due to epinephrine secretion. Glycogenolysis occurs in the liver and muscle tissues and helps to increase glucose stores available for cellular use.
bottomLine: During the stress response, a metabolic cascade of events occurs in an attempt to provide the body with needed energy. This puts the body in a relative catabolic state. In modern medicine, these often are a detriment to the patient. In the surgical period, decreasing the degree of the stress response can help influence postoperative outcome.

Posterior --> antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin.

stem: Which of the following is the PRIMARY goal of denitrogenation prior to the induction of anesthesia?

options.text: Maximizing dissolved oxygen content in the arterial blood
options.html: Maximizing dissolved oxygen content in the arterial blood

options.text: Maximizing oxygen content in the functional residual capacity
options.html: Maximizing oxygen content in the functional residual capacity

options.text: Maximizing oxygen content in the inspiratory reserve volume
options.html: Maximizing oxygen content in the inspiratory reserve volume

explanation: The primary goal of denitrogenation (preoxygenation) is to displace the nitrogen in the functional residual capacity (FRC) with oxygen to provide an oxygen reserve for the apneic period. Removal of nitrogen from the FRC increases the content of oxygen available for apneic oxygenation after induction of anesthesia. With room air-breathing, 95% of the FRC is filled with nitrogen which provides little reserve of oxygen during apnea. Denitrogenation is most successfully employed by breathing 90% to 100% O2 with a tight-fitting oxygen mask at 10 to 12 L per minute of flow at normal tidal volumes. Time to desaturation to SpO2 of <90% in healthy nonobese patients can be greater than eight minutes vs only one to two minutes without denitrogenation. In patients with obesity, respiratory gas exchange impairment, elevated oxygen consumption (eg, neonates), or restricted lung volumes, this is even more important because the time to desaturation in these individuals is limited, even with adequate denitrogenation. Results of one study provided evidence that the time to desaturation in patients with obesity who had adequate denitrogenation was only 2.7 minutes versus six minutes in nonobese patients.
rationales:
Dissolved arterial oxygen content does not contribute substantially to apneic oxygen reserves due to the poor solubility of oxygen in the blood.
Answer C: The inspiratory reserve volume is the volume above the tidal volume inspiration with maximal inhalation effort. This volume does not contribute to oxygen reserves during apneic periods.
bottomLine: Denitrogenation (preoxygenation) of the functional residual capacity allows a greater apneic oxygenation time during the induction of anesthesia.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Denitrogenation Primary Goal (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Airway Management. Page 768. 7th editon.

stem: Which of the following factors is MOST LIKELY responsible for the release of arginine vasopressin?
explanation: Vasopressin is also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and arginine vasopressin (AVP). An increase in plasma osmolality will lead to secretion of the hormone. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is an endogenous peptide made in the hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei that is stored in the posterior lobe of the pituitary. There are certain conditions that either stimulate its release or inhibit its release. Two of the most important factors responsible for secretion of AVP are hyperosmolality and reduced effective circulating volume. Other factors that stimulate its release include: angiotensin II, stress, pain, nausea, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, and certain drugs like nicotine. Factors that inhibit its release are hypoosmolality, increased effective circulating volume, cortisol, and drugs such as caffeine. AVP stimulates water resorption by increasing intracellular levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and activating protein kinase A. It also stimulates vasoconstriction by activating G protein and phospholipase C, which releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. There are two classes of AVP receptors: V1 receptors present in vascular smooth muscle and V2 receptors present in the distal and collecting tubules of the kidney. AVP is metabolized by the kidneys and liver after its release into the plasma. Its half-life is 15-20 minutes.
rationales:
Caffeine would inhibit the release of AVP.
Answer B: ADH (AVP) hypersecretion occurs in cortisol deficiency. Cortisol deficiency results in increased hypothalamic secretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), an ADH secretagogue. Cortisol feeds back negatively on CRH and ACTH, an inhibitory effect that is removed with adrenal insufficiency. Both cortisol and antidiuretic hormone are released in response to surgical stress, but it should be noted that cortisol appears to directly suppress ADH secretion.
Answer C: Increasing effective circulating volume would inhibit the release of AVP.
bottomLine: AVP is the main physiologic factor in water resorption. It is released from the pituitary in response to hyperosmolality, reduced effective circulating volume, angiotensin II, stress, pain, nausea, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, and certain drugs.

stem: Which of the following hormones is cleaved intravascularly during passage through the pulmonary circulation?
explanation: Angiotensin I (AI) is cleaved and converted to Angiotensin II (AII) in the pulmonary circulation by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Renin is produced in the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney and secreted into the circulation in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure. Renin (a protease) cleaves circulating angiotensinogen (globulin made in the liver) into angiotensin I. Angiotensin I travels into the pulmonary circulation, where ACE cleaves AI into AII. Angiotensin II has multiple physiologic effector sites including the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal glands, where the secretion of aldosterone is promoted. Angiotensin II serves to increase vascular and sympathetic tone and raise the intravascular volume.
rationales:
Angiotensin I is cleaved and converted to Angiotensin II in the pulmonary circulation by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE).
Answer C: Epinephrine is also not affected by pulmonary circulation.
bottomLine: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by intravascular ACE in the pulmonary circulation.

stem: Carbon dioxide is primarily transported in blood in which of the following three forms?

options.text: Dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds
options.html: Dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds

options.text: Dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and methyl carbamate
options.html: Dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and methyl carbamate

options.text: Dissolved CO2, carbonic acid, and carbamino compounds
options.html: Dissolved CO2, carbonic acid, and carbamino compounds

explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO2)is transported in the blood as dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds. Carbon dioxide is 10 times more soluble in blood than in oxygen: 0.031 mmol/L/mmHg vs 0.003 mmol/L/mmHg, respectively. Despite this, most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate. This occurs because red blood cells and vascular endothelium contain carbonic anhydrase, an enzyme used to convert CO2 to bicarbonate. The enzyme also catalyzes the reverse reaction. In both cases, the transient intermediate carbonic acid is created. Bicarbonate production: H2O + CO2 ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3−. Carbamino compounds also transport CO2 in the blood. Carbamino compounds are produced from a reaction with proteins. The small amount of CO2 transported in this manner mostly interacts with hemoglobin proteins and, to a lesser extent, plasma proteins. Carbamino compound production: R-NH2 + CO2 → R-NH-CO2- + H+.
rationales:
Methyl carbamate is not related to CO2 transport.
Answer C: The full reaction proceeds so quickly that blood never contains appreciable quantities of carbonic acid.
bottomLine: Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood as dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carbon Dioxide: Blood Transport" Marino PL. The ICU Book. 3rd edition.

stem: Which of the following statements about bronchial smooth muscle tone is TRUE?

options.text: ß2 adrenergic receptor stimulation causes bronchial constriction
options.html: ß2 adrenergic receptor stimulation causes bronchial constriction

options.text: Epinephrine acts on ß1 adrenergic receptors to cause bronchial dilation
options.html: Epinephrine acts on ß1 adrenergic receptors to cause bronchial dilation

options.text: Muscarinic receptor stimulation causes bronchial dilation
options.html: Muscarinic receptor stimulation causes bronchial dilation

options.text: Norepinephrine does not cause significant bronchial dilation
options.html: Norepinephrine does not cause significant bronchial dilation

explanation: Norepinephrine is more selective for β1 receptors than β2 and accordingly, does not cause significant bronchial smooth muscle relaxation.
rationales:
Bronchial smooth muscle relaxes in response to β2 adrenergic stimulation leading to bronchial dilation.
Answer B: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are the two endogenous catecholamines responsible for sympathetic stimulation but are differentially selective for the β-adrenergic receptors. Epinephrine acts at both β1 and β2 and causes significant bronchial smooth relaxation and bronchodilation.
Answer C: Bronchial smooth muscle contracts in response to muscarinic (M3) stimulation causing bronchial constriction.
bottomLine: Stimulation of β2 adrenergic receptors causes bronchodilation while M3 receptor stimulation causes bronchoconstriction. Epinephrine causes significant bronchodilation. Norepinephrine does not cause significant bronchial smooth muscle relaxation as it is more β1-selective.

stem: Which of the following occurs during ventricular diastole?
explanation: Diastasis is a slow filling which occurs during ventricular diastole. It is the second of three phases of ventricular filling. The cardiac cycle, discussed mainly from the standpoint of the ventricles, consists of diastole and systole. Ventricular diastole involves filling of the ventricles and can be broken down into isovolumetric relaxation followed by filling. Isovolumetric relaxation starts with the closure of the aortic valve and ends with the opening of the mitral valve signaling the onset of filling. The filling phase is further broken down into early rapid filling, diastasis (also called slow filling), and then atrial systole. Early rapid filling is caused by negative intracavitary pressure in the ventricle created by fast myocardial relaxation. This is referred to as diastolic suction. Ventricular systole follows atrial systole starting with isovolumetric contraction marked by the closure of the mitral valve. Once intraventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens, and the ejection phase of systole begins. As blood is ejected and pressure falls, the aortic valve will close marking the start of diastole with isovolumetric relaxation. Diastole and systole are coordinated by the cardiac conduction system. The sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the posterior wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, is the pacemaker for a healthy heart. When it fires, electrical signals travel through the atria causing the atria to depolarize and enter atrial systole. The electrical signal travels to the atrioventricular (AV) node where it experiences a pause before moving onto the conduction system in the ventricles. From the AV node, the signal is conducted through the Bundle of His, to the right and left bundle branches, and then through the Purkinje fibers. Overlap occurs between atrial systole and ventricular diastole with the atria entering systole and contributing to ventricular filling while the ventricles are still in diastole. A delay in the conduction system at the AV node allows the ventricles time to fill from the atria before entering systole themselves. As the electrical current moves from the AV node into the ventricles, the ventricles will start to contract entering systole. Wiggers diagram, illustrating cardiac cycle.
rationales:
Isovolumetric contraction occurs during ventricular systole. It starts with the closure of the mitral valve and continues as pressure builds enough to cause the opening of the aortic valve, signaling the end of isovolumetric contraction and the start of ejection.
Answer C: The Purkinje fibers are part of the ventricular conduction system. When an action potential reaches the Purkinje fibers, the ventricles start to contract signaling the start of ventricular systole.
bottomLine: The cardiac cycle, discussed mainly from the standpoint of the ventricles, consists of diastole and systole. Ventricular diastole starts with isovolumetric relaxation following by rapid filling, diastasis (slow filling), and atrial systole. Ventricular systole starts with isovolumetric contraction followed by ejection of the blood from the ventricles.

stem: During laparoscopic surgery, which of the following is LEAST likely to occur secondary to carbon dioxide embolism?

options.text: End-tidal CO2 decreases secondary to hemodynamic instability
options.html: End-tidal CO2 decreases secondary to hemodynamic instability

options.text: End-tidal CO2 increases secondary to vascular CO2 insufflation
options.html: End-tidal CO2 increases secondary to vascular CO2 insufflation

options.text: Hemodynamic improvement with discontinuation of nitrous oxide
options.html: Hemodynamic improvement with discontinuation of nitrous oxide

explanation: Most serious cases of carbon dioxide embolism reported in the literature occurred at the beginning of the procedure due to misplacement of the Veress needle (pneumoperitoneum needle) directly into a vein or parenchymal organ. Carbon dioxide embolism can manifest similar to an air embolus, causing obstruction to RV ejection, right and left cardiac failure, paradoxical embolism, arrhythmia, pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypotension, and cardiovascular collapse. Review of the literature varies as to the lethal volume of CO2, but it is likely between 600 mL to 1750 mL in an adult. A gas bubble composed of 100% CO2 will not enlarge in a patient inhaling 50% or even 75% N2O because CO2 is more soluble than N2O. CO2 will, therefore, move out or be absorbed or buffered more quickly than N2O will move in. This is not to deny that N2O should not be discontinued if CO2 embolism is suspected, but hemodynamic improvement will not typically be seen in the immediate period. Several reports have shown an increase in ETCO2 with hemodynamically unstable carbon dioxide embolism. One particular report showed a continuously recorded ETCO2 concentration that increased abruptly from 3.8 to 4.2% in carbon dioxide embolism patients who were diagnosed on the basis of a sudden abrupt onset of systolic and diastolic murmurs during laparoscopy. Another report showed a temporal association of cardiovascular collapse with an abrupt increase in ETCO2. Most reports, however, described significant decreases in ETCO2 with clinical episodes of carbon dioxide embolism. Answers A & B: Carbon dioxide embolism may increase or decrease PETCO2. Other effects include elevated pulmonary arterial pressure, elevated central venous pressure, hypoxemia, and increased PCO2.
rationales: Hyperventilation (especially with 100% O2) increases carbon dioxide excretion and decreases the volume of the embolus.
bottomLine: Discontinuation of N2O does not improve hemodynamic stability with 100% CO2 embolus. However, it should be discontinued to provide 100% oxygen during cardiopulmonary compromise. Decreased ETCO2 is more commonly seen, but increased ETCO2 may occur in CO2 embolus even in cardiovascular collapse.

stem: Compared to the baseline values shown in the blue left ventricular pressure-volume loop below, which of the following points in the diagram represents a shift toward INCREASED lusitropy?
explanation: Lusitropy is defined as the rate of active myocardial relaxation. Positive (increased) lusitropy may be represented by a downward and rightward shift in the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR) curve of a pressure-volume loop, which is best illustrated by the curve corresponding to point A. In this state, increased myocardial compliance is demonstrated by an increased left ventricular end-diastolic blood volume for a given end-diastolic pressure. Pressure-volume (PV) loops may be used to illustrate the operating conditions of the heart by plotting the pressures within a ventricular chamber as a function of the volume within the ventricle throughout the cardiac cycle. The PV loop changes its shape and position in response to certain physiologic parameters, such as afterload, preload, inotropy, and lusitropy. A state of positive (or increased) lusitropy is observed when a more compliant ventricle with a greater rate of relaxation tolerates a higher end-diastolic volume at a lower end-diastolic pressure. This relationship is illustrated on the PV loop via a downward and rightward shift of the slope at the end of diastole (end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship or EDPVR). By contrast, an increase in preload would be indicated by rightward movement of the PV loop along the same EDPVR slope, as greater blood volume is subject to slightly higher pressures given the same degree of lusitropy. Meanwhile, an upward shift of the entire EDPVR curve would indicate decreased compliance or negative lusitropy. The end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) is represented by the upper left curve and is linear under physiologic conditions. The slope of the ESPVR serves as an index of myocardial contractility (inotropy). Accordingly, a decrease in inotropy would be represented as a downward and rightward shift of the ESPVR. This is not to be confused with an increase in afterload, which would be associated with greater end-systolic pressures and a higher end-systolic volume, causing the PV loop to translate upward and to the right along the same ESPVR curve. As an example, congestive heart failure with pure left ventricular systolic dysfunction would be seen as a downward shift in the ESPVR, signifying decreased contractility or negative inotropy. To maintain stroke volume, sympathetic activation and fluid retention would cause an increase in left ventricular volume, and end-diastolic pressures might increase as a result (producing a rightward translation of the PV loop along EDPVR slope). An individual can also exhibit decreased left ventricular contractility and decreased compliance simultaneously, which would substantially reduce stroke volume. For instance, such conditions may arise in the event of an acute myocardial infarction involving a large portion of the left ventricular wall, which would place the patient at risk of cardiogenic shock.
rationales:
Point B illustrates negative lusitropy compared to the baseline value. The end-diastolic pressure is therefore higher for a given end-diastolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient with significant diastolic dysfunction (e.g., profound concentric left ventricular hypertrophy).
Answer C: Point C illustrates negative inotropy compared to the baseline value. The end-systolic pressure is therefore lower for a given end-systolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient with significant systolic dysfunction (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy due to left ventricular scarring).
Answer D: Point D illustrates positive inotropy compared to the baseline value. The end-systolic pressure is therefore higher for a given end-systolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient administered an inotropic drug such as dobutamine or milrinone.
bottomLine: Pressure-volume loops can be used to illustrate changes in cardiac work due to changes in ventricular pressure as a function of ventricular volume. Positive lusitropy is depicted by a rightward and downward shift of the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship curve, which illustrates a more compliant ventricle that can accommodate larger volumes at decreased pressures.
trueLearnInsight: In an average adult, a normal EDV (end-diastolic volume) and ESV (end-systolic volume) might be approximately 120 and 40-50 mL, respectively. Stroke volume (EDV-ESV) is therefore ~70-80 mL or ~60-67% in a normally functioning heart.

stem: Which of the following would result in INCREASED oxygen delivery to the tissues?
explanation: A right-shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve results in hemoglobin’s decreased affinity for oxygen, resulting in increased oxygen delivery to tissues, as occurs with hyperthermia, hypercarbia, and acidemia. A left-shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve results in hemoglobin’s increased affinity for oxygen, resulting in decreased oxygen delivery to tissues, as occurs in the presence of fetal hemoglobin, methemoglobinemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, or hypophosphatemia (a substrate for the production of 2,3-DPG). Oxygen delivery to the tissues can be calculated with the equation: DO2 = CO * CaO2 CO = cardiac output CaO2 = arterial oxygen content Where CaO2 = [1.34 * Hgb * SaO2] + [PaO2 * 0.003] Hgb = hemoglobin concentration SaO2 = arterial oxygen saturation PaO2 - arterial partial pressure of oxygen Oxygen delivery is also affected by factors that affect the P50, the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (the normal P50 is 27 mm Hg). This value is a marker of hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and is used to evaluate changes in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, which reflects the amount of oxygen delivery to tissues.
rationales:
CO binds to hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin, which increases oxygen affinity of the remaining heme sites. This results in a left-shifted oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, with reduced oxygen delivery.
Answer B: Hypophosphatemia commonly occurs secondary to sepsis, malnutrition, refeeding syndrome, acute liver injury, and diabetic ketoacidosis (due to increased urinary phosphate excretion). Inorganic phosphate is a substrate for 2,3-DPG production, and if hypophosphatemia is not corrected, the decreased 2,3-DPG results in an increased affinity of oxygen for hemoglobin, a left-shifted oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and reduced oxygen delivery.
bottomLine: Oxygen delivery is dependent on cardiac output and arterial oxygen content, but is also affected by factors influencing the P50, the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated. A left-shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin desaturation curve results in increased oxygen affinity and decreased oxygen delivery, whereas a right-shift results in decreased oxygen affinity and increased oxygen delivery to tissues.

stem: Which of the following would MOST likely be found in a patient with cyanide toxicity?
explanation: The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Cyanide primarily causes toxicity by impairing cellular aerobic respiration. The cyanide ion (CN-) binds to the ferric ion (Fe3+) in mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, inhibiting the final stage of the electron transport chain. Depletion of cellular ATP and the lactic acid produced by anaerobic metabolism can lead to profound acidosis. Symptoms of cyanide toxicity include altered mental status, weakness, headaches, loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure, and cardiac arrest. Blood cyanide levels will be elevated, although therapy should not be delayed for the laboratory result. The patients blood sample may appear "cherry red" due to normal circulating levels of oxygen with impaired utilization.
rationales:
Circulating oxygen is not impaired and cyanosis is a late finding.
Answer B: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. Therefore, PaO2 will increase.
Answer C: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. SvO2 will be increased.
bottomLine: The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis.
trueLearnInsight: Anion gap is calculated by subtracting serum chloride and bicarbonate (anions) from serum sodium and potassium (cations). Anion gap = ([Na+] +[K+]) – ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). In clinical practice, potassium is usually excluded.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 910, 1077. Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition, p. 2501. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cyanide Toxicity: Dx"

stem: Which of the following is NOT true regarding the stress response and lipolysis?

options.text: Lipolysis is increased by alpha-2 stimulation
options.html: Lipolysis is increased by alpha-2 stimulation

options.text: Lipolysis is increased by beta-2 adrenergic stimulation
options.html: Lipolysis is increased by beta-2 adrenergic stimulation

options.text: Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines
options.html: Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines

explanation: Alpha-2 stimulation will inhibit lipolysis. The stress response occurs when the body is placed under surgical or traumatic strain. The stress response is categorized by loss of fat and lean body mass. The response is termed an ‘obligate’ catabolic state which results in proteolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, hypermetabolism, and insulin resistance. This state is not reduced by exogenous nutrition as would occur in a fasting state. The body's response to surgery and trauma depends on the magnitude of injury, surgical time, and degree of postoperative pain. Lipid metabolism is altered during stress. Lipolysis is the hydrolysis of triglycerides into glyceride and free fatty acids which are then used as an energy source. In general, lipolysis is increased by beta-2 and beta-3 adrenergic stimulation but is inhibited by alpha-2 stimulation. Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines when compared to men.
rationales:
Lipolysis is increased by certain catecholamines - beta-2 adrenergic stimulation will increase lipolysis.
Answer C: Increased catecholamines, cortisol, and glucagon secretion all promote lipolysis.
Answer D: Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines.
bottomLine: During the stress response, lipolysis increases in response to catecholamine stimulation. Lipolysis is the hydrolysis of triglycerides into glyceride and free fatty acids.

stem: Which of the following statements describes the hepatic arterial buffer response?

options.text: Hepatic arterial vasoconstriction in response to hypercarbia
options.html: Hepatic arterial vasoconstriction in response to hypercarbia

options.text: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to hypoxemia
options.html: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to hypoxemia

options.text: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to increased local nitric oxide
options.html: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to increased local nitric oxide

options.text: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to reduced portal venous flow
options.html: Hepatic arterial vasodilation in response to reduced portal venous flow

explanation: The hepatic arterial buffer response (HABR) is responsible for maintaining constant hepatic blood flow. Through the action of the HABR, changes in portal venous flow induce reciprocal changes in hepatic arterial flow. With an intact HABR, as portal venous blood flow decreases, the hepatic artery vasodilates resulting in increased hepatic arterial flow. The opposite occurs when portal venous blood flow increases. Changes in hepatic artery blood flow do not induce reciprocal changes in the portal venous system. The key player in the HABR is adenosine. Adenosine is produced in the space of Mall surrounding the local hepatic vasculature and diffuses into the portal vein. As portal venous blood flow decreases, the decreased flow allows the accumulation of adenosine in the hepatic vasculature. This increased concentration of adenosine causes vasodilation of the hepatic artery and increased hepatic arterial blood flow. As portal venous flow increases, the increased flow washes the adenosine out of the hepatic vascular system resulting in vasoconstriction of the hepatic artery. This is known as the “adenosine wash-out hypothesis.” The maximum effect of the HABR can double the hepatic arterial blood flow. The response can be abolished by endotoxemia and splanchnic hypoperfusion. The liver gets 20-25% of the cardiac output via the portal vein and the hepatic artery. The portal vein is responsible for 75% of the blood flow while the hepatic artery is responsible for 25% of the blood flow. However, both vascular structures each deliver 50% of the oxygen supply to the liver.
rationales:
Hypercapnia can modulate the blood flow within the hepatic vasculature; however, this does not describe the hepatic arterial buffer response.
Answer B: Decreases in oxygen tension of the portal venous system can result in increased hepatic arterial blood flow. Arterial hypoxemia can modulate liver blood flow. However, these are not qualities of the hepatic arterial buffer response.
Answer C: Nitric oxide has no role in the hepatic arterial buffer response. However, nitric oxide does play a role in regulating the resistance of the liver sinusoids. Cirrhosis can cause a disruption of the liver sinusoids and a resultant decrease in the activity of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). This results in decreased nitric oxide and may contribute to the development of portal hypertension. On the other hand, nitric oxide production is increased in the mesenteric vasculature during portal hypertension causing splanchnic hyperemia.
bottomLine: With a functioning hepatic arterial buffer response, hepatic arterial tone is modulated by portal venous flow, via adenosine, in order to maintain hepatic perfusion.
trueLearnInsight: Glucagon causes dose-dependent hepatic arterial vasodilation. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction of hepatic arterial and portal venous systems. Vasopressin increases splanchnic vasoconstriction while decreasing resistance to portal venous flow.

stem: An alteration of which of the following parameters MOST significantly stimulates the carotid body chemoreceptors?

options.text: Arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide
options.html: Arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide

explanation: Carotid body chemoreceptors are primarily responsive to reductions in arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2). The carotid bodies are located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries bilaterally and contain afferent glossopharyngeal nerve branches that become stimulated in response to reductions in PaO2. Once the PaO2 falls below 60-65 mm Hg, neural activity increases to augment minute ventilation. Once the PaO2 increases to above 65 mm Hg, the neural input to the central respiratory centers ceases. Ventilation then falls again until the decrease in PaO2 surpasses this threshold again. Answers A & B: The carotid bodies are not stimulated by changes in arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) or arterial oxygen content (CaO2).
rationales:
Alterations in arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) do not stimulate the carotid body receptors sufficiently to produce changes in minute ventilation.
Answer E: The carotid body chemoreceptors do show some response to reductions in pH, however, the response is minor.
bottomLine: The carotid body chemoreceptors are located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries bilaterally. The chemoreceptors are stimulated to increase minute ventilation in response to decreases in PaO2 below 60-65 mm Hg.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carotid body: hypoxic drive" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 240.

stem: A 68-year-old alcoholic male comes in for emergent evacuation of subdural hematoma after a fall while intoxicated 1 hour ago. He is agitated, not following commands, and icteric on exam. The family states he has a history of cirrhosis and is noncompliant with medication therapy. He has no other medical history and is not taking any other medications. Which of the following is MOST likely true regarding his liver disease?

options.text: Albumin level is better than INR for the evaluation of liver synthetic function
options.html: Albumin level is better than INR for the evaluation of liver synthetic function

options.text: Decreased factor VIIa reflects poor liver synthetic function
options.html: Decreased factor VIIa reflects poor liver synthetic function

options.text: Elevated direct bilirubin suggests poor synthetic hepatic function
options.html: Elevated direct bilirubin suggests poor synthetic hepatic function

options.text: Transaminase levels best reflect the current functional status of his liver
options.html: Transaminase levels best reflect the current functional status of his liver

explanation: Synthetic liver function is best assessed via the INR or PT which most closely correlates with factor VIIa levels. INR is the best lab value to assess hepatic synthetic function as it correlates with factor VIIa levels, which only have a half-life of 4 hours and thus will reflect acute or chronic declines in hepatic synthetic function reliably. This is obviously confounded in situations where the INR will be elevated for other reasons such as warfarin therapy, vitamin K deficiency, dilutional coagulopathy, or other coagulopathies. The other test used to assess hepatic synthetic function is albumin. Albumin is synthesized by the liver however it has a half-life of approximately 3 weeks (therefore not particularly useful for acute evaluation) and its value can be normal in cirrhosis or be decreased for a multitude of reasons such as poor nutrition, albumin catabolism, volume overload, and protein losing nephropathy.
rationales:
INR is superior to albumin in the assessment of hepatic synthetic function.
Answer C: Direct, or conjugated bilirubin, increases when there is a disruption with bile removal such as choledocolithiasis and would in fact reveal that the liver has the ability to convert unconjugated to conjugated bilirubin. It is not useful in the evaluation of hepatic synthetic function.
Answer D: Transaminase levels better reflect liver injury and can be normal or low in severe cirrhosis where most of the liver parenchyma is destroyed. It is not a very useful test to evaluate liver synthetic function.
bottomLine: Synthetic liver function is best assessed via the PT/INR, which most closely correlates with factor VIIa levels.

stem: Which of the following is a source of tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide poisoning?

options.text: Left shift of the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve
options.html: Left shift of the oxygen hemoglobin dissociation curve

explanation: Tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning can occur due to a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. This occurs as a result of hemoglobin’s (Hb) increased affinity for CO as compared with oxygen. This leftward shift therefore increases oxygen binding to the Hb molecule. Carbon monoxide poisoning is commonly associated with burn victims due to smoke exposure during a fire. Carbon monoxide has an affinity for Hb that is 200-300 times stronger than oxygen. Hemoglobin preferentially binds to CO (carboxyhemoglobin, or COHb) leaving less Hb available for oxygen to bind. In addition, oxygen that binds with Hb tends not to dissociate from Hb, resulting in a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. CO disrupts mitochondrial function, which leads to less adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production as a result of uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Combined, these factors result in tissue hypoxia and a metabolic acidosis (with an anion gap). Clinically, CO poisoning is difficult to discover without an adequate history because oxygen saturation is usually normal. Standard pulse oximetry is unable to distinguish between COHb and oxyhemoglobin as they both absorb light at similar frequencies. The diagnosis of carbon monoxide poisoning is made by co-oximetry, when elevated levels of COHb (> 15%) are found on arterial or venous blood gas analysis. Treatment includes high FiO2 which helps displace CO. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for patients with COHb > 30% and/or severe symptomatology (e.g., obtundation, delirium, bradyarrhythmia, etc.).
rationales:
CO disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to less ATP production due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
Answer C: The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production.
bottomLine: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia and acidosis by decreased coupling of oxidative phosphorylation, a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreased ATP production, and increased lactate production.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding the rate of induction of anesthesia in the setting of intracardiac shunts is TRUE?

options.text: Inhalational induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt
options.html: Inhalational induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt

options.text: Inhalational induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt
options.html: Inhalational induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt

options.text: Intravenous induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt
options.html: Intravenous induction is more rapid with a left-to-right intracardiac shunt

options.text: Intravenous induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt
options.html: Intravenous induction is slowed with a right-to-left intracardiac shunt

explanation: Inhalational induction is delayed in the setting of a right-to-left intracardiac shunt. The rate of inhalational anesthetic induction is determined by minute ventilation, functional residual capacity, blood/gas solubility, cardiac output, cerebral blood flow, and the presence of intracardiac shunts. A right-to-left intracardiac shunt delays inhalational induction since the volatile anesthetic-rich blood returning to the left heart is diluted by volatile anesthetic-poor systemic venous blood from the right heart. In addition, the uptake of inhaled anesthetics is prolonged with a right-to-left shunt due to a decrease in pulmonary blood flow. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected.
rationales:
The rate of inhalational induction is virtually unchanged in the setting of left-to-right intracardiac shunting.
Answer C: The rate of intravenous induction in the setting of left-to-right shunt is decreased minimally, or not changed at all, due to increased recirculation of drugs into the pulmonary circulation.
Answer D: Intravenous induction is accelerated in the setting of right-to-left intracardiac shunting due to a partial bypass of the pulmonary circulation.
bottomLine: Speed of induction in the setting of intracardiac shunts. stem: Stimulation of which of the following is MOST likely to cause reflex bronchoconstriction?
explanation: Reflex bronchoconstriction is due to parasympathetic stimulation that occurs through the vagus nerve. Reflex bronchoconstriction is a result of the activation of parasympathetic nerves derived from the vagus (CN X) nerve. Sensory afferent nerves in the airway are activated, which send signals to the nucleus of the solitary tract. Efferent signals are sent via parasympathetic nerves, which release acetylcholine, activating both M2 and M3 (muscarinic) receptors on the smooth muscle in the bronchi and bronchioles. Activation of M3 receptors leads to smooth muscle contraction and bronchoconstriction. To prevent excessive bronchoconstriction, prejunctional inhibitory M2 receptors are also activated, which limits the degree of acetylcholine release. Reflex bronchoconstriction can occur with stimuli such as methacholine, cold air, histamine, allergens, and exercise.
rationales:
Stimulation of β-adrenergic receptors causes bronchodilation.
Answer B: There are two types of non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) neurons in the lungs (inhibitory and excitatory). Inhibitory NANC neurons cause bronchodilation through the effects of peptides such as vasoactive intestinal peptide and nitric oxide. Excitatory NANC neurons are responsible for bronchoconstriction and are activated by neuropeptides such as substance P and neurokinin A. These neuropeptides also stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system in the lungs.
Answer C: Stimulation of muscarinic, not nicotinic, receptors leads to bronchoconstriction.
bottomLine: Reflex bronchoconstriction is a result of the activation of parasympathetic nerves derived from the vagus (CN X) nerve.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Reflex Bronchoconstriction: Neurons" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Ch. 14: Autonomic Nervous System Anatomy and Physiology: Lungs. 8th edition. Gropper MA, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Ch. 44: Airway Management in the Adult: Airway Reflexes and the Physiologic Response to Intubation of the Trachea. 9th edition. Drake MG, et al. Airway Sensory Nerve Plasticity in Asthma and Chronic Cough. Front Physiol. 2021 Sep 7;12:720538. UpToDate. Neuronal Control of the Airways. Literature review current through Aug 2022. This topic last updated May 04, 2022.

stem: A 60-year-old male with no significant past medical history is in the PACU after an uneventful total knee arthroplasty under general anesthesia. You are called to evaluate the patient for declining SpO2 which is currently 85% on a 2L nasal cannula. He is awake and following commands, breathing at a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute, and does not appear to be breathing deep or shallow. An arterial blood gas is drawn which reveals the following values: pH: 7.28 PaCO2: 60 mm Hg PaO2: 55 mm Hg HCO3: 27 mEq/L Which of the following statements is MOST likely true?

options.text: Critical closing pressure of the upper airway is decreased
options.html: Critical closing pressure of the upper airway is decreased

options.text: The patient likely had a prior carotid right endarterectomy
options.html: The patient likely had a prior carotid right endarterectomy

explanation: This patient has hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory insufficiency related to opioids, benzodiazepines, and volatile anesthetic administration with a decrease in glossopharyngeal afferent nerve activity due to impairment of the carotid body chemoreceptors. Unlike CO2 chemoreception, which is mostly central with a smaller peripheral component, PaO2 sensing is purely peripheral, mainly occurring in the carotid bodies, which are paired structures located at the point of carotid bifurcation. PaO2 chemoreceptors can provide a very strong stimulus to the central pattern generator (i.e. pontomedullary network) via the glossopharyngeal nerves and nucleus tractus solitarii. However, since such strong stimulation is only triggered by hypoxic conditions with PaO2 ~55 mmHg, it is not commonly seen under physiological conditions (one example would be at high altitude where climbers with no supplemental oxygen will hyperventilate in spite of respiratory alkalosis). In addition, more recent studies found that the carotid bodies are not silent under normoxic conditions, rather they provide tonic stimulation to the central pattern generator. Because the carotid bodies are very sensitive to inhibition by volatile anesthetics, even at subanesthetic concentrations down to 0.1 MAC, and because the central pattern generator contributes to maintenance of upper airway patency (for example by stimulating the genioglossus muscle), it is likely that volatile-induced inhibition of the carotid bodies can contribute to postoperative airway obstruction in patients at risk such as those with obstructive sleep apnea.
rationales:
The critical closing pressure of the upper airway (Pcrit) is the pressure proximal to the velopharynx at which complete airway collapse occurs with no inspiratory flow during spontaneous breathing. For example if a patient is requiring 5 cm H2O CPAP to prevent complete collapse of the upper airway, then his/her Pcrit at this time is 5 cm H2O. Pcrit is negative in awake individuals, becomes less negative during sleep and often becomes positive during anesthesia
Answer C: Bilateral carotid endarterectomy would result in a similar phenomenon, however, this patient has no history of medical issues, and there is no mention of prior neck surgery or scarring, and thus it would be less likely than medication induced impairment of hypoxic ventilatory drive.
Answer D: The vagus nerve provides innervation to the aortic body which does have a very minimal contribution to control of hypoxic ventilatory drive but not to the extent that the carotid body does and its activity is likely decreased not increased.
bottomLine: The carotid body chemoreceptors increase ventilation when PaO2 (not PAO2, CaO2, or SaO2) decreases through afferent impulses via the glossopharyngeal nerve to CNS ventilation centers. Their function is impaired by opioids, benzodiazepines, volatile anesthetics (as low as 0.1 MAC), and bilateral carotid endarterectomy.
trueLearnInsight: Do not confuse carotid bodies and carotid sinuses. Both are located at the carotid bifurcation, and impulses from both are transmitted via a branch of the glossopharyngeal (Hering’s nerve) but carotid bodies are chemoreceptors while carotid sinuses are baroreceptors.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carotid Body: Hypoxic Drive" Miller’s Anesthesia, 8th Edition, Chapter 27, pages 687-697 Dempsey JA, Smith CA. Pathophysiology of human ventilatory control. Eur Respir J. 2014 Aug;44(2):495-512

stem: Which of the following values is NOT required to calculate static respiratory system compliance?
explanation: Peak pressure is used to calculate dynamic respiratory system compliance (C). The static compliance of the respiratory system indicates the “stiffness” of the respiratory system, which includes the lungs and chest wall. It is determined at the end of inspiration when there is no airflow, hence “static.” This can be accomplished, for example, during an inspiratory pause in a mechanically ventilated patient. Since compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in pressure of a system (C = ΔV/ΔP), the following formula is used to calculate static respiratory system compliance: CS = VT ÷ (PPL – PEEP) Where: CS is static compliance, VT is tidal volume, and PPL is plateau pressure. Dynamic respiratory system compliance, which is also a reflection of respiratory system resistance, can be measured at any point during inspiration when there is airflow. Commonly, dynamic compliance is measured using peak pressure during inspiration, the value of which simply replaces plateau pressure in the above formula.
bottomLine: Static respiratory system compliance is calculated using the following formula: CS = VT ÷ (PPL – PEEP).
trueLearnInsight: Elastance is the inverse of compliance: E = ΔP/ΔV.
references: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 236-237. Hess DR, Bigatello LM. The chest wall in acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. Curr Opin Crit Care. 2008 Feb; 14(1): 94-102. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pulmonary compliance: Calculation"

stem: A patient presents to the emergency department with an acute ischemic stroke. An angiogram shows occlusion of the left anterior cerebral artery. What is the most likely presenting symptom?
explanation: The anterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the medial surface of the parietal lobe, which includes part of the primary motor cortex. The part of the cortex which is located medially, is that which gives motor function to the lower limb (B). The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) is a branch off of the internal carotid artery. It supplies blood to the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, the anterior 4/5 of the corpus collosum, the anterior portions of the basal ganglia and internal capsule, and the olfactory bulb and tract. ACA infarcts are rare, representing only 2% of ischemic strokes. The functional areas supplied by the ACA are: - Prefrontal cortex: functions in motivation, planning, and organizing of complex behavior - Supplemental motor area (dominant cortex): functions with Broca’s area for speech - Motor cortex (lower limb) - Sensory cortex (lower limb) ACA strokes on the left can lead to behavioral abnormalities as well as aphasia. Sensory and motor deficits are also commonly seen, but they are more often seen in the lower limb due to the anatomical division of the motor and sensory cortex, where the area of the cortex supplying the lower limb is medial (see picture of motor homunculus below). Right sided ACA strokes, on the other hand, can lead to left leg weakness and sensory deficits, behavioral abnormalities, and left hemineglect. explanationHtml:
The anterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the medial surface of the parietal lobe, which includes part of the primary motor cortex. The part of the cortex which is located medially, is that which gives motor function to the lower limb (B).

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) is a branch off of the internal carotid artery. It supplies blood to the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, the anterior 4/5 of the corpus collosum, the anterior portions of the basal ganglia and internal capsule, and the olfactory bulb and tract.

ACA infarcts are rare, representing only 2% of ischemic strokes.

The functional areas supplied by the ACA are: - Prefrontal cortex: functions in motivation, planning, and organizing of complex behavior - Supplemental motor area (dominant cortex): functions with Broca’s area for speech - Motor cortex (lower limb) - Sensory cortex (lower limb) ACA strokes on the left can lead to behavioral abnormalities as well as aphasia.

Sensory and motor deficits are also commonly seen, but they are more often seen in the lower limb due to the anatomical division of the motor and sensory cortex, where the area of the cortex supplying the lower limb is medial (see picture of motor homunculus below).

Right sided ACA strokes, on the other hand, can lead to left leg weakness and sensory deficits, behavioral abnormalities, and left hemineglect.

stem: A 72-year-old female with postoperative oliguria has a plasma osmolality of 294 mOsm/kg. Which of the following urine osmolality values suggests a prerenal cause to this patient's oliguria?
explanation: A urine-to-plasma osmolar ratio (UOSM: POSM) >1.5 indicates prerenal oliguria (generally secondary to hypovolemia). In this patient, the urine osmolality would need to be >441 mOsm/kg (294 mOsm/kg x 1.5) (E). The UOSM: POSM is used to assess the tubular response of the kidneys to dehydration or hypovolemia. In this setting of prerenal oliguria, this formula evaluates the kidneys’ ability to retain Na+ and water and produce highly concentrated urine by increasing urine osmolality above 450 mOsm/kg. By comparison, normal plasma osmolality is 280-300 mOsm/kg. The UOSM: POSM indicates the kidneys' ability to concentrate urine. Tubular damage and acute renal failure, therefore, may be represented by a decreased ratio. The UOSM: POSM can also decrease with the administration of diuretics. As an aside, isosthenuria is a UOSM: POSM equal to 1. Answers A & B & C & D: In this patient, the urine osmolality would need to be >441 mOsm/kg (294 mOsm/kg x 1.5).
bottomLine: A UOSM: POSM ratio >1.5 is indicative of prerenal oliguria secondary to dehydration or hypovolemia. The UOSM: POSM evaluates the ability of the kidneys to concentrate urine and increase urine osmolality above normal plasma osmolality in the setting of prerenal oliguria.
references: Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, p. 455. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Prerenal Oliguria Dx/Rx"
