stem: Which of the following will MOST likely facilitate the release of oxygen from hemoglobin?

options.text: Transfusion of packed red blood cells
options.html: Transfusion of packed red blood cells

explanation: The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (ODC) describes the relationship between arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) and the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2). The sigmoid curve that results from the cooperative binding of oxygen. This means that, when one molecule of oxygen binds to the hemoglobin, the affinity of the hemoglobin for the next oxygen molecule increases. Each hemoglobin can bind up to four oxygen molecules. The ODC can signify changes in hemoglobin affinity for oxygen by shifting either to the left or to the right. A leftward shift is associated with increased hemoglobin affinity, while a rightward shift is associated with decreased hemoglobin affinity. One way to measure the shift of the curve is by referring to the P50 value, which is the oxygen tension (PaO2) when SaO2 is 50%. A normal P50 value is 27 mmHg. A leftward shift will result in a lower P50 value, and a rightward shift will result in an increase in P50 value. Abbreviations: DPG, diphosphoglycerate; Hb, hemoglobin; PO2, partial pressure of oxygen; Temp, temperature. When the affinity of hemoglobin is low (rightward shift), more oxygen molecules can be unloaded from the hemoglobin into the tissues. In normal physiology, the ODC is shifted to the left at the level of the lungs where oxygen molecules must be picked up by the hemoglobin. As the oxygenated blood approaches the level of the tissues, the ODC shifts to the right, allowing these molecules of oxygen to unload. The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen is affected by many factors. Temperature, hydrogen ion concentration, partial pressure of CO2 (PaCO2), and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) cause the ODC to shift either left or right. • Left shift (P50 < 27): seen with a decrease in temperature, PaCO2, 2,3-DPG, and hydrogen ion concentration (high pH) • Right shift (P50 > 27): seen with an increase in temperature, PaCO2, 2,3-DPG, and hydrogen ion concentration (low pH) Abbreviations: CAD, coronary artery disease; DPG, diphosphoglycerate; H+, hydrogen ion; PaCO2, partial pressure of arterial oxygen; PRBC, packed red blood cell. Other factors, such as drugs, diseases, and electrolytes, can change the affinity of the hemoglobin by affecting the concentration of 2,3-DPG: • Thyroxine has been shown to stimulate the production of 2,3-DPG, causing a rightward shift of the ODC. • Hyperphosphatemia stimulates 2,3-DPG production (rightward shift), while hypophosphatemia decreases 2,3-DPG (leftward shift). • 2,3-Diphosphoglycerate is also increased (rightward shift) in anemia, high-altitude hypoxia, heart failure, liver cirrhosis, and sleep apnea syndrome. • Propranolol causes a rightward shift of the ODC in patients with coronary artery disease, without affecting 2,3-DPG. • Stored packed red blood cells have decreased 2,3-DPG, resulting in a leftward shift.
rationales:
A decrease in hydrogen ion concentration (high pH) causes a leftward shift of the ODC.
Answer C: Myxedema coma, a complication of hypothyroidism, presents with low thyroxine and hypothermia. This results in a leftward shift of the ODC.
Answer D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells causes the ODC to shift to the left due to decreased levels of 2,3-DPG.
bottomLine: A leftward shift of oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is caused by a decrease in temperature, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2), hydrogen ion concentration, and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG). A rightward shift is caused by an increase in temperature, PaCO2, hydrogen ion concentration, and 2,3-DPG.
trueLearnInsight: Remember the mnemonic "CADET Face Right". Increase in CO2, Acid, 2,3-Diphosphoglycerate, Exercise, and Temperature result in Right shift. Cadets prefer to unload their guns (oxygen).

stem: A 50-year-old man weighing 70 kg is in the critical care unit after a motor vehicle accident in which he experienced multiple rib fractures, thoracic spine fractures, and pulmonary contusion bilaterally. He is currently intubated and mechanically ventilated. Which of the following is MOST true regarding the renal effects of positive pressure ventilation?

options.text: Positive pressure ventilation increases sympathetic output, which will increase urine output
options.html: Positive pressure ventilation increases sympathetic output, which will increase urine output

options.text: Secretion of antidiuretic hormone would be greater if the patient did not require positive pressure ventilation
options.html: Secretion of antidiuretic hormone would be greater if the patient did not require positive pressure ventilation

options.text: Tidal volume of 6 mL/kg could decrease renal injury by decreasing cytokine release
options.html: Tidal volume of 6 mL/kg could decrease renal injury by decreasing cytokine release

explanation: Decreasing the tidal volume to 6 mL/kg (lung-protective strategy) could decrease the risk of renal injury related to positive pressure in the patient in this question by decreasing cytokine release. Multiple reports of studies have linked renal and lung injury together through multiple mechanisms. The ARDSnet trial provided evidence that lung-protective ventilation decreases the incidence of hemodynamic, coagulopathic, and renal complications with a lung-protective strategy. Unfortunately, renal effects secondary to mechanical ventilation are not as simplistic as alterations in cytokine release. Strategies employed to target specific renal consequences from positive pressure ventilation have not been proven effective. Renal effects from mechanical ventilation involve 3 broad categories: hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and biochemical. Induction of positive pressure ventilation affects hemodynamics by decreasing preload and increasing right ventricular afterload (both of which decrease cardiac output and renal blood flow) while promoting increased venous pressure, all of which have deleterious effects on the kidneys. Positive pressure ventilation also results in an increase in sympathetic nervous system output, which secondarily results in an increase in renin release through beta-1 receptor stimulation with resultant release of angiotensin-2 and aldosterone. This results in vasoconstriction with salt and water retention, which can decrease urine output. There is also an increase in the release of antidiuretic hormone (also seen with surgical stress), which increases free water reabsorption and decreases urine output; however, this is a minor component. Finally, there is a decrease in atrial natriuretic peptide, which decreases natriuresis and vasodilation. Biochemically, positive pressure ventilation induces cytokine release, which can cause endothelial activation, increase vascular permeability, and result in apoptosis of renal epithelial cells. The pattern of ventilation can have alterations in the amount of cytokine release and resultant renal injury as previously discussed regarding the ARDSnet trial. There is also evidence that positive pressure ventilation increases the release of nitric oxide and enhances nitric oxide synthase activity. The breakdown products of nitric oxide cause oxidative damage and increased vascular permeability and can result in cellular apoptosis.
rationales:
Sympathetic output is increased with positive pressure ventilation; however, this leads to decreased urine output.
Answer B: Antidiuretic hormone secretion would be decreased compared to a patient on positive pressure ventilation.
bottomLine: Positive pressure ventilation exerts deleterious effects on renal function via alterations in hemodynamics, neurohormonal secretion, and biochemical mediator release.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Mechanical Ventilation: Renal Effects" Koyner JL, et al. Mechanical Ventilation and Lung-Kidney Interaction. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2008 Mar;3(2):562-570.

stem: Which of the following compounds is synthesized by the liver?
explanation: The liver is responsible for the synthesis and release of angiotensinogen. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is one of the primary regulators of volume and blood pressure. Angiotensinogen circulates in the plasma until cleaved by renin to form angiotensin I. Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus in response to β1 activation, decreased renal perfusion pressure (glomerulus), or decreased NaCl concentration at the macula densa (distal convoluted tubule). Angiotensin I is cleaved to form the active angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lungs. There are a multitude of biological compounds produced by the liver; many are shown in the table below. Notably, factor 3 (tissue factor), factor 4 (calcium), von Willebrand factor (endothelium), tPA, and platelets (megakaryocytes) are not primarily synthesized by the liver. Glucose (gluconeogenesis) Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) Antithrombin III Plasminogen
rationales:
Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is released from the heart in response to myocardial stretch receptors in the right and left ventricles similarly to atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) released from the atria. Both ANP and BNP cause vasodilation, natriuresis/diuresis, and inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in response to volume overload states (CHF, cirrhosis, renal failure, right heart failure). BNP causes inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase in the collecting ducts to promote sodium excretion.
Answer C: Platelets are synthesized and released by megakaryocytes, which are produced in the bone marrow. Of note, thrombopoietin (TPO) is produced by the liver and stimulates bone marrow release of megakaryocytes. Thrombocytopenia is a common finding in cirrhosis given a deficiency of TPO and hypersplenism.
Answer D: VWF is synthesized from the Weibel-Palade bodies and subendothelium. Desmopressin (or DDAVP) is sometimes used to facilitate the release of vWF in coagulopathic patients or in patients with von Willebrand disease via activation of the V2 receptor.
bottomLine: Angiotensinogen is synthesized in the liver. The majority of clotting factors are synthesized and released from the liver with notable exceptions of factors 3, 4, and von Willebrand factor. Platelets are synthesized by megakaryocytes in the plasma.
trueLearnInsight: Factor VIII is synthesized in the liver as well as endothelial cells. Thus, it remains at normal (or high) levels when other factors are deficient in liver disease.

stem: A patient has a respiratory system compliance of 100 mL/cm H2O and a lung compliance of 200 mL/cm H2O. What is the patient’s chest wall compliance?

options.text: Cannot be determined without additional information
options.html: Cannot be determined without additional information

explanation: Compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in pressure of a system (C = ΔV/ΔP) which is the inverse of elastance (E = ΔP/ΔV). The compliance (or elastance) of the respiratory system is dependent on the compliance (or elastance) of the lungs and the chest wall. Elastance of the respiratory system is simply the sum of its two components, but since compliance is the inverse of elastance: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW Where C is compliance, RS is respiratory system, L is lungs, and CW is chest wall. Therefore, using the above values, the CCW can be calculated: 1/CCW = 1/CRS – 1/CL 1/CCW = 1/100 – 1/200 = 2/200 – 1/200 1/CCW = 1/200 CCW = 200 Although it is unlikely to be encountered for testing purposes, CCW is directly calculated using the formula below: CCW = VT ÷ (PPL – PATM) Where VT is tidal volume, PPL is pleural pressure, and PATM is atmospheric pressure. However, under most circumstances PATM = 0 (except in the setting of negative pressure such as from an "iron lung" ventilator), so the calculation can be simplified: CCW = VT ÷ PPL Answers A & C & D: 1/CCW = 1/CRS – 1/CL = 1/200
bottomLine: The following formula summarizes the relationship of respiratory system compliance and its two components: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW.
trueLearnInsight: Chest wall compliance is relatively high in neonates due to a pliable rib cage. However, this increases work of breathing since the rib cage provides less mechanical support, which in turn leads to significant retractions and earlier functional airway closure.

stem: Which of the following would INCREASE minimum alveolar concentration requirements for an adult patient?
explanation: Hypernatremia increases minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) values for a patient. Factors increasing MAC: Drugs - Amphetamine (acute use) - Cocaine - Ephedrine - Ethanol (chronic use) Age - Highest at age 6 months Electrolyte disturbance - Hypernatremia Hyperthermia Factors decreasing MAC: Drugs - Propofol, etomidate, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, ketamine - Alpha-2 agonists (clonidine, dexmedetomidine) - Ethanol (acute use) - Local anesthetics - Opioids - Amphetamines (chronic use) - Lithium - Verapamil Age - >65 years Electrolyte disturbance - Hyponatremia Others - Anemia (hemoglobin <5 g/dL) - Hypercarbia - Hypothermia - Hypoxia Pregnancy
rationales:
Acute alcohol use decreases MAC.
Answer B: Hypercarbia decreases MAC.
bottomLine: Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) can be affected by electrolyte disturbances. Hypernatremia increases MAC.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents for an open inguinal hernia repair to be performed under general anesthesia. Which of the following compounds at a moderate concentration in the blood is MOST likely to reduce renal blood flow without changing the glomerular filtration rate?
explanation: Epinephrine is a potent vasoconstrictor and would be expected to decrease renal blood flow without increasing the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). While renal blood flow is autoregulated under normal physiologic conditions, it is also greatly impacted by other factors. The sympathetic nervous system provides constant baseline vascular tone, and, as sympathetic output (including the release of epinephrine) increases, renal afferent tone increases as well, which reduces blood flow to the kidney. Renal blood flow is also regulated by the renin-angiotensin system. Renin, a molecule released by the renal system in times of low blood flow, converts angiotensinogen in the bloodstream to angiotensin I. In the pulmonary system, this is further converted to angiotensin II, which is a potent vasoconstrictor. However, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent renal vasculature, thereby relatively increasing GFR but also decreasing the renal blood flow. At very high levels of activation, angiotensin II loses its preferential effects on the efferent vasculature and reduces renal blood flow by strongly constricting the afferent and efferent vasculature. Angiotensin II also promotes the release of aldosterone, which increases sodium and water resorption, leading to higher blood pressure in general. Finally, various other local and hormonal factors also influence renal blood flow, including the vasodilators nitric oxide, prostaglandins, and atrial natriuretic peptide.
rationales:
Although angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, the efferent arterioles will preferentially be affected, thereby increasing the GFR while slightly reducing the renal blood flow. Additionally, the increase in systemic blood pressure caused by angiotensin II will also help to maintain renal perfusion. At supraphysiologic levels, angiotensin II will constrict both afferent and efferent vasculature, thereby reducing renal blood flow.
Answer B: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released from the atria in response to high filling pressures. Atrial natriuretic peptide is a vasodilator of the afferent arterioles and a vasoconstrictor of the efferent arterioles and will, therefore, increase blood flow to the kidneys when it is released in response to stretching of the atria.
bottomLine: The sympathetic nervous system provides baseline vascular tone in the kidney and, when it is activated, causes vasoconstriction that can decrease renal blood flow.
trueLearnInsight: Inhaled anesthetics cause transient, reversible depression in renal function. Glomerular filtration rate, renal blood flow, urine output, and urinary excretion of sodium are decreased.

stem: Rapid and excessive normal saline administration would MOST likely result in which of the following sets of lab values? Plasma bicarbonate Plasma chloride Strong ion difference Anion gap A ↓ ↑ ↓ normal B ↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ C ↓ ↑ normal normal
explanation: Excessive and rapid administration of normal saline can lead to a nonanion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with decreased plasma bicarbonate (HCO3−), increased plasma chloride (Cl−), and a decreased plasma strong ion difference (SID). Normal (0.9%) saline solution contains 154 mEq each of Na+ and Cl−. It has a strong ion difference of 0 because both sodium and chloride are strong ions. Normal human plasma has a SID of 40 to 44 mEq/L. Therefore, rapid administration of normal saline will cause a decrease in SID (by decreasing from 40 to 44 mEq/L closer to 0), leading to acidemia. The concept of SID proposes that plasma pH is determined by three independent factors: PCO2, SID, and total plasma concentration of nonvolatile buffers (Atot). The latter (Atot) represents the total plasma concentration of nonvolatile buffers (eg, albumin, globulins, and inorganic phosphate). Strong ion difference represents the difference between the charge of plasma strong cations (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium) and anions (chloride and other strong anions [A−] such as lactate, sulfate, ketoacids, and nonesterified fatty acids). SID = ( [Na+] + [K+] + [Ca2+] + [Mg2+] ) - ( [Cl−] + [A−] ) ≈ 40 to 44 mEq/L. The increase in Cl−is compensated for by a decrease in HCO3−. The anion gap, therefore, typically remains in a normal range. Anion Gap = ([Na+] + [K+]) - ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). Therapy for saline-induced hyperchloremic acidosis consists of intravenous administration of a crystalloid solution with a high SID, such as sodium bicarbonate or tromethamine ("Tham" solution).
rationales:
The SID will decrease, not increase, and the anion gap will be largely unchanged.
Answer C: The SID will decrease, not increase, due to the strong ion difference of normal saline being 0 mEq/L and the normal strong ion difference of the plasma being 40 mEq/L. A large volume infusion of normal saline will bring the normal 40 mEq/L closer to 0 mEq/L.
bottomLine: Large volumes and rapid administration of normal saline can produce a nonanion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Associated laboratory values include decreased plasma HCO3−, increased plasma Cl−, decreased strong ion difference, and a normal anion gap.

stem: Oxygen unloading is decreased in which of the following scenarios?
explanation: Fetal hemoglobin shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, which decreases oxygen unloading allowing fetal hemoglobin to hold onto oxygen more tightly. This improves oxygen delivery to the fetus from the placenta. Causes of right shift include increases in factors such as pCO2, acidity or [H+] (so a decreased pH), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), exercise, and temperature. Leftward shifts are due to decreases in these factors as well as increases in carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia, and HbF (fetal hemoglobin). Oxygen is primarily transported in the blood via hemoglobin in red blood cells. It is also dissolved to a much lesser degree. The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) and the % oxygen saturation of hemoglobin (SaO2). The graphical relationship between these 2 variables can best be described as sigmoidal shaped due to cooperative binding which refers to the phenomenon of oxygen binding further increasing the affinity for additional oxygen molecules to bind to the hemoglobin. The P50 refers to the oxygen tension at which the hemoglobin is 50% saturated. Under normal circumstances, P50 in adults is 26.7 mmHg. Several factors can alter the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen which results in a left or right shift on the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. Decreased affinity is represented by a rightward shift and is characterized by increased oxygen displacement from hemoglobin to be released to other tissues. The P50 is also increased with a rightward shift. Causes of right shift include increases in pCO2, acidity or [H+] (so a decreased pH), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), exercise, and temperature. 2,3-DPG is formed in red blood cells and is part of an adaptive mechanism in which its production is increased in the presence of anemia or hypoxia. The rightward shift associated with increased 2,3-DPG levels allows more oxygen to be released at peripheral tissues. An increase in CO2 resulting in a rightward shift is known as the Bohr effect. Hemoglobin's increased affinity for oxygen is represented by a leftward shift and is associated with a lower P50. Leftward shifts can be caused by opposite changes compared to rightward shifts including decreases in pCO2, acidity or [H+], 2,3-DPG, and temperature. Low levels of 2,3-DPG can be seen in states such as sepsis and hypophosphatemia. Additionally, since hemoglobin binds to carbon monoxide around 240 times more readily compared to oxygen, the presence of carbon monoxide results in a leftward shift. Methemoglobinemia also shifts the curve to the left. Lastly, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is structurally different from normal hemoglobin and the dissociation curve for HbF is relatively leftward shifted. Fetal arterial oxygen partial pressures are low and the left shift increases oxygen uptake at the placenta. HbF persists in a newborn until about 2-4 months of age and is usually completely replaced by adult hemoglobin at 6 months.
rationales:
Increased 2,3-DPG concentration causes a shift to the right.
Answer C: Alkalosis causes a shift to the left. This decreases the dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin (holds on to oxygen). Acidosis would shift the curve to the right.
bottomLine: Hyperthermia, acidosis, high pCO2, and high levels of 2,3-DPG cause a shift to the right. Fetal hemoglobin shifts the curve to the left.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Oxyhemoglobin Right Shift (B)" Miller Anesthesia. Chapter 19: Respiratory Physiology and Pathophysiology. 8th Edition. Page 445. Image sources: Wikimedia Commons. Image: Oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve.png. Accessed 17-Sep-2019. Available at: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Oxyhaemoglobin_dissociation_curve.png

stem: Which of the following increases minimum alveolar concentration of inhaled anesthetics?
explanation: The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhaled anesthetics is increased by use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI). Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Other factors include increasing age (especially > 40), hypoxia, hypothermia, induced hypotension, anemia, and certain drugs including α-2 agonists, lithium, large doses of cholinesterase inhibitors, lidocaine, opioids, barbiturates, and calcium channel blockers. By contrast, there are fewer factors that increase MAC. These include hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g., as caused by MAOIs, acute amphetamine use, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa). In general, those factors that decrease central nervous system (CNS) metabolic activity, neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and down-regulate CNS responses to chronically elevated neurotransmitter levels decrease MAC. Those factors that increase CNS metabolic activity and neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and up-regulate CNS responses to chronically depressed neurotransmitter levels increase MAC. Answers A & B & D & E: Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia.
bottomLine: Hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g. MAOIs, amphetamine, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa use) increase MAC requirements for anesthetic agents.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC / Factors That Increase, Decrease" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 424-425.

stem: Which of the following will lead to increased oxygen delivery?
explanation: Increasing hemoglobin increases arterial oxygen content, which will lead to increased oxygen delivery, assuming no concurrent changes in cardiac output. Oxygen delivery (DO2) is determined by the equation: DO2 = CO x CaO2, where CO is cardiac output and CaO2 is arterial oxygen content. Therefore, an increase in either CO or CaO2 will increase oxygen delivery. Each component of this equation can be further broken down to illustrate various physiologic effects on oxygen delivery. CaO2 = [(SaO2)(Hb x 1.34)] + (0.0031 x PaO2) Where: SaO2 is arterial oxygen saturation, Hb is hemoglobin, PaO2 is partial pressure of arterial oxygen. Assuming all other variables remain stable, this equation illustrates that when SaO2, Hb (A), or PaO2 increase, CaO2 and, therefore DO2 increase. Note, however, that increases in PaO2 usually produce a negligible increase in CaO2. Any decrease in CO will result in a decrease in oxygen delivery. Cardiac output can be described by several different equations. At its simplest: CO = HR x SV, where HR is heart rate and SV is stroke volume. This shows that increases in HR or SV can increase DO2, again assuming all other variables remain constant. Stroke volume, in turn, is determined by cardiac preload, afterload, and contractility. Increasing cardiac preload or cardiac contractility or decreasing cardiac afterload will increase CO (if the heart rate remains stable) and therefore DO2. Alternately, CO can be represented by: CO = BP / SVR, where BP is systemic blood pressure and SVR is systemic vascular resistance. Accordingly, as SVR increases, CO decreases if there is not a compensatory increase in blood pressure.

Increasing SVR alone will decrease the CO (by increasing the afterload) and reduce DO2.

stem: Assuming normal cardiopulmonary function, which of the following statements regarding the relationship of partial pressures (P) of inhaled anesthetics at equilibrium is CORRECT?
explanation: When cardiopulmonary function is normal (absence of shunting), PCNS = Pblood = Palveoli. The goal of delivering inhaled anesthetics is to produce the anesthetic state by establishing a specific concentration of anesthetic molecules in the central nervous system (CNS). This is done by establishing the specific partial pressure of the agent in the lungs, which ultimately equilibrates with the brain and the spinal cord. For inhaled anesthetics at equilibrium, CNS partial pressure (PCNS) equals blood partial pressure (Pblood), which in turn equals alveolar partial pressure (Palveoli). This equilibration is primarily the result of three factors. Inhaled anesthetics are gasses that are rapidly transferred bidirectionally via the lungs to and from the bloodstream and subsequently to and from CNS tissues as partial pressures equilibrate. Plasma and tissues have a low capacity to absorb the inhaled anesthetics relative to the amount one can deliver to the lungs, allowing one to quickly establish or abolish anesthetizing concentrations of anesthetic in the bloodstream and ultimately the CNS. Metabolism, excretion, and redistribution of the inhaled anesthetics are minimal relative to the rate at which they are delivered or removed from the lungs; this permits easy maintenance of blood and CNS concentrations. Answers A & B: The relationships between PCNS, Pblood, and Palveoli are not additive and are not associated with a gradient at equilibrium.
bottomLine: As long as normal cardiopulmonary function exists (i.e. no intrapulmonary, intracardiac, or cardiopulmonary shunting), PCNS = Pblood = Palveoli of inhaled anesthetics at equilibrium.
references: American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Anesth partial pressures at equilibrium" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 415.
